core: Definition of a glacier: a mass of ice that forms on land and flows under its own weight
Glacier formation: snow accumulation exceeding melting, burial, compaction through firn to ice
Accumulation vs ablation balance and the equilibrium line; advance and retreat of glacier fronts
Glacier types: valley (alpine) glaciers, ice sheets, ice caps, ice shelves
Glacier movement: internal deformation and basal sliding
Glacial erosion and landforms: U-shaped valleys, cirques, arêtes; depositional forms: moraines, drumlins, erratics
Why glaciers matter: freshwater storage, sea-level connection, ice cores as climate archives
supporting: Ice-age context: Last Glacial Maximum roughly 20,000 years ago
Firn as the intermediate stage between snow and glacial ice
Glaciers as part of the water cycle and the cryosphere
outOfScope: Climate and climate change (sibling topics 'climate', 'climate-change'; referenced only)

claims.claim: A glacier is a mass of ice and snow that forms on land and flows slowly downhill under its own weight; USGS adds that it is a perennial accumulation that also carries rock, sediment, and often liquid water.

Glaciers form where winter snowfall exceeds summer melting year after year; the weight of accumulated snow compresses buried snow, first into firn and then into glacial ice, a process that takes over a hundred years for most glaciers.

A glacier has a zone of accumulation, where snowfall exceeds melting, and a zone of ablation, where melting and calving remove more ice than snow adds; the equilibrium (firn) line marks the boundary, and summer melt matters most to the glacier's budget.

Valley (alpine) glaciers flow down mountain valleys; ice sheets are continent-scale masses of land ice larger than 50,000 square kilometers, and today only the Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets exist; ice caps are smaller dome-shaped glaciers under 50,000 square kilometers; ice shelves are floating extensions of land ice over a cold coastal ocean.

The Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets together contain more than 99 percent of the freshwater ice on Earth and about 68 percent of Earth's fresh water; almost 10 percent of Earth's land area is covered by glaciers and ice caps.

Glaciers move by internal deformation, in which ice flows plastically under its own weight (with the rigid upper ice carried along by the flowing ice below), and by basal sliding, in which a film of meltwater lets the ice slide over its bed; where the bed is frozen, movement is by internal flow alone.

A glacier's front advances when the forward flow of ice outpaces melting and calving, stays roughly stationary when they balance, and retreats when melting and calving outpace flow; ice within the glacier keeps moving even while the front retreats.

Glacial erosion is done mostly by rock fragments embedded in the ice, which grind and pluck the bedrock; alpine glaciers carve U-shaped valleys, cirques, arêtes, and horns, while continental glaciation tends to smooth broad bedrock surfaces.

Glacial deposition produces till (unsorted sediment) and landforms including moraines (ridges of unsorted sediment piled at a glacier's edges, including the terminal moraine marking its farthest advance), drumlins (streamlined mounds shaped like an inverted canoe), and erratics (rocks carried far from their origin and left by melting ice).

Global average sea level has risen about 8 to 9 inches (21 to 24 centimeters) since 1880, driven mostly by meltwater from glaciers and ice sheets together with thermal expansion of seawater as it warms.

Ice cores drilled from polar ice sheets and mountain glaciers preserve layered records of past climate; proxy indicators including oxygen isotopes, methane concentrations, and dust content are used to reconstruct climate history.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sea-level rise if the entire Antarctic Ice Sheet melted
positions: Open Textbook BC Physical Geology (16.2): about 80 meters, with most major cities submerged
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Estimates differ with the modeling assumptions used. The lesson does not use either Antarctic-only figure; it uses the NOAA-verified global statement (sea level up about 8-9 inches / 21-24 cm since 1880, mainly from glacier and ice-sheet meltwater plus thermal expansion), which is supported by the cited NOAA page and consistent with the NSIDC figures.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Share of Earth's fresh water held in the Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets
positions: NSIDC: more than 68 percent of the fresh water on Earth
Open Textbook BC Physical Geology (16.2): approximately 68 percent
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both sources agree within rounding; the lesson states 'about 68 percent' and cites both.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Share of Earth's land covered by glaciers and ice caps
positions: USGS Water Science School: almost 10 percent
NSIDC: world's glaciers (excluding the ice sheets) total roughly 700,000 square kilometers, with most glacier ice in Antarctica
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The USGS figure is used for land coverage because it is the checked statement in the source; NSIDC's separate figures for the ice sheets and world glacier area are used where area is discussed. Both are cited and consistent in magnitude.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft is generic boilerplate ('Glaciers is a foundational concept in Earth & Space Science...') and makes no substantive factual claims about glaciers, so no draft claims carried forward.
Draft framing of a glacier as a 'label on a toolbox drawer' was discarded as non-substantive.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced all machine-generated boilerplate with original, source-verified lesson content.
Used the USGS glacier definition (perennial land ice moving under its own weight) and the NSIDC flow definition rather than a vague 'frozen water' characterization.
Excluded the Antarctic-only sea-level-rise figure (60 m vs 80 m disagreement between sources) in favor of the NOAA global sea-level statement, which is unambiguous and Tier A verified.
Kept climate change strictly as a reference (sibling topic) and did not teach climate attribution or projections.

sourceRecords.title: Glaciers and Icecaps — Water Science School
sourceRecords.notes: Read live (https://www.usgs.gov/special-topics/water-science-school/science/glaciers-and-icecaps). Supports: glacier definition (perennial accumulation of crystalline ice, snow, rock, sediment, and often liquid water that originates on land and moves down slope under its own weight and gravity); formation where snowfall far exceeds summer melting, with compaction by the weight of accumulated snow; 'almost 10 percent of the world's land mass' covered by glaciers and ice caps; Yosemite Valley as a classic U-shaped glacial valley; glaciers as freshwater storehouses and part of the water cycle. Facts synthesized into original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Glaciers — Parts of the Cryosphere
sourceRecords.provider: National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC), University of Colorado Boulder
sourceRecords.notes: Read live. Supports: glacier as an accumulation of ice and snow that slowly flows over land; higher-elevation snow surplus driving downhill flow; snow to firn (about two-thirds the density of water after about a year) to glacial ice over more than a hundred years for most glaciers; Last Glacial Maximum roughly 20,000 years ago; ice-sheet definition (>50,000 km2 / 19,300 mi2) and the only two remaining ice sheets (Antarctic ~14 million km2, Greenland ~1.7 million km2, both averaging ~2 km thick); ice caps as dome-shaped glaciers under 50,000 km2; Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets holding more than 99 percent of freshwater ice and over 68 percent of Earth's fresh water; world glacier area ~700,000 km2. Figures unit-checked in Python against the source's own conversions.

sourceRecords.title: Ice Shelves — Parts of the Cryosphere
sourceRecords.provider: National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC), University of Colorado Boulder
sourceRecords.notes: Read live. Supports the ice-shelf definition used in the lesson: extensions of thick land ice that flow out over a cold coastal ocean, roughly 50 to 600 meters thick, with most of the world's ice shelves fringing the Antarctic coast. Facts synthesized into original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Climate Change: Global Sea Level
sourceRecords.notes: Read live (served as the archived version of NOAA Climate.gov as of June 25, 2025; article by Rebecca Lindsey, published August 22, 2023). Supports: global average sea level risen 8-9 inches (21-24 cm) since 1880, mostly from meltwater from glaciers and ice sheets plus thermal expansion of seawater; the 2006-2015 rate of 0.14 inches (3.6 mm) per year being about 2.5 times the twentieth-century average of 0.06 inches (1.4 mm) per year. Conversion figures (21-24 cm to inches, mm/yr to in/yr) verified in Python.

sourceRecords.title: Ice Core — NCEI Paleoclimatology
sourceRecords.provider: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live. Supports the claim that ice cores from polar and low-latitude mountain glaciers and ice caps preserve proxy climate indicators including oxygen isotopes, methane concentrations, and dust content, used to reconstruct past climate. Lesson mentions ice cores as archives of past climate without teaching climate-change science (sibling topic).

sourceRecords.title: 16.2 How Glaciers Work — Physical Geology (2nd ed.)
sourceRecords.provider: BCcampus Open Education / Open Textbook BC
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture of 2024 (live site blocks automated fetch). Supports: two main glacier classes (continental vs alpine/valley); zones of accumulation and ablation and the equilibrium line; snow to firn to glacial ice by compression; summer melt dominating the glacier budget; internal deformation (plastic flow of ice below about 50-100 m) and basal sliding on a meltwater film, with frozen-bed glaciers moving by internal flow alone; front advance/stability/retreat as flow vs ablation balance; calving; Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets holding about 99 percent of glacial ice and approximately 68 percent of Earth's fresh water. Facts synthesized into original prose.

sourceRecords.title: 16.3 Glacial Erosion — Physical Geology (2nd ed.)
sourceRecords.provider: BCcampus Open Education / Open Textbook BC
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture of 2024 (live site blocks automated fetch). Supports: erosion by rock fragments embedded in ice (sandpaper analogy) rather than by the ice itself; U-shaped valleys with relatively flat bottoms and steep sides; cirques as bowl-shaped basins at the head of a glacial valley; arêtes as sharp ridges between U-shaped valleys; horns; drumlins as elongated features streamlined at the down-ice end; continental glaciation smoothing broad bedrock surfaces. Facts synthesized into original prose.

sourceRecords.title: 16.4 Glacial Deposition — Physical Geology (2nd ed.)
sourceRecords.provider: BCcampus Open Education / Open Textbook BC
sourceRecords.notes: Reused existing registry id (identical URL). Read via Wayback Machine capture (live site blocks automated fetch). Supports: till as sediment transported and deposited by glacial ice, unsorted and spanning a wide range of grain sizes; end moraines as ridges of unsorted sediment formed at a stationary glacier's melting front; the terminal moraine marking the glacier's farthest advance; lodgement till deposited beneath moving ice. Facts synthesized into original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Glossary of Glacier Terminology — Open-File Report 2004-1216
sourceRecords.notes: Read live (text version). Supports the lesson's landform and process vocabulary: cirque (bowl-shaped, amphitheater-like depression eroded into the head or side of a glacier valley); arête (jagged, narrow ridge separating two adjacent glacier valleys or cirques); ice sheet (thick, subcontinental to continental-scale ice spreading from a center of accumulation); ice cap (dome-shaped accumulation completely covering a mountainous area or island); erratic (rock transported a significant distance by a glacier or iceberg and deposited by melting, from pebble-size to larger than a house); drumlin (streamlined, inverted blunt-ended canoe shape); moraine types (lateral, ground, end, terminal); firn line separating accumulation and ablation zones. Definitions synthesized into original prose.
